name: Additive manufacturing for end-use production
summary: Industrial 3D printing produces qualified final parts with geometries, customisation or production volumes that are difficult to serve economically with conventional methods.
useCase: A medical supplier repeatedly manufactures patient-specific implants, or an aerospace company produces a qualified lightweight component with fewer assembly steps.
whyNow: The relevant transition is from printing an impressive prototype to consistently supplying useful parts. Wohlers reports global additive-manufacturing revenue of $20.035 billion in 2023 and $24.2 billion in 2025. Its 2026 review says services grew faster than system sales, suggesting that utilisation and paid production matter more than simply shipping machines. That market total includes prototyping, equipment, materials and software, so it overstates the narrower end-use-production opportunity. Successful applications exploit geometry, low-volume economics, part consolidation or customisation. The process must still deliver qualified material properties, traceability, finishing and inspection at an acceptable total cost per part.

mainstream.scope: Routine serial manufacture of selected medical, aerospace, industrial tooling and high-value spare parts where additive processes have a demonstrable design or cost advantage.
mainstream.rationale: Commercial end-use applications already exist. More repeatable process control, qualification and manufacturing services can widen the economically useful range before 2030. Commodity high-volume parts often remain better suited to other methods, so the date does not imply universal replacement of machining, casting or moulding.

metric.name: Global additive-manufacturing industry revenue
metric.scope: Wohlers global AM market estimate, including equipment, services, materials and software; a broader-market proxy for end-use production.
metric.limitations: Nominal revenue is affected by prices, reporting coverage and product mix. It is not the value of end-use parts alone or a share of total manufacturing. No intermediate value is interpolated. Prefer the report’s stated 10.9% 2025 growth when discussing that single year.
metric.futureNote: No defensible comparable external deployment forecast found. The separate maturity path is an analyst scenario, not measured adoption.
metric.growthLabel: 2025 total AM revenue +10.9%; end-use subset not separately measured

milestones.text: Wohlers’ 2022 report describes a 19.5% rebound in industry revenue in 2021; that is all additive manufacturing, not only final parts.
Wohlers’ subsequent comparison recorded 3,049 metal AM systems sold, a hardware metric kept separate from industry revenue.
Wohlers estimated $20.035 billion global AM revenue and 3,793 metal systems sold.
The 2024 report stressed materials qualification, certification and lower part costs as drivers of end-use production.
Global AM revenue reached $24.2 billion, with printing services the largest revenue segment.
Wohlers introduced a more continuously updated market-intelligence platform and emphasised utilisation and production outcomes. The $24.2 billion figure still describes 2025.

tailwinds: Complex geometries and part consolidation can create functional advantages unavailable from a simple process substitution.
Customisation and low-volume production can avoid expensive dedicated tooling.
Digital inventories and qualified service bureaus can shorten selected spare-parts lead times.
bottlenecks: Qualification, inspection and post-processing can dominate total cost and delivery time.
Build-to-build consistency and traceable material properties are essential in regulated products.
Machine and material economics vary greatly by part geometry and annual volume.
watchMetrics: Revenue and repeat orders for qualified end-use parts, separated from prototype and hardware sales.
Total delivered cost, scrap rate and throughput for the same qualified part.
Machine utilisation, customer retention and the number of designs in sustained serial production.
